extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of rules for patent validity (utility / principle / embodiment) and for measuring/recovering damages for infringement, with illustrations from case law. Focuses on what is patentable, when patents are void for lack of utility or deception, temporal scope of infringement, and how damages are assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / Usefulness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must possess some utility; the subject-matter must be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject-matter of a patent is more or less useful it is immaterial so long as it possesses some utility. If the subject-matter consists of several things all included in one patent but claimed as distinct inventions, a failure of any one of them in point of utility must vitiate the patent. (Examples and cases discussed: distinctions between an invention useful 'on the whole' vs. where the purpose wholly fails.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial failure vs. total failure of claimed usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding that an invention is useful 'on the whole' but fails or is not useful in some cases is not a ground for nonsuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the jury finds the invention 'is new and useful upon the whole' but that 'in some cases it is not useful,' the court will generally infer usefulness in the generality of cases and will not hold the patent void unless the purpose wholly fails and the invention does not accomplish the effect claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for a bare principle — embodiment required
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a patent for a principle alone; a principle must be embodied and applied so as to afford some practical utility in the arts and manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A principle 'reduced into practice' or the 'practice founded on principle' (i.e., the manufacture or thing done or made) is the subject-matter of a letters-patent. The legal inquiry is into the spirit/principle of the invention as embodied in some mode or method; mere abstract truth or law is not patentable unless clothed with a form producing the claimed benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions among types of 'principles' and implications for scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles may be truths of exact science, laws of natural science, or rules of practice; these classes differ and affect how an inventor may appropriate an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truths of exact science and laws of natural science exist independently of human operation and cannot be appropriated per se; protection extends to the particular embodiment/application. Rules of practice originate with humans and may partake more of invention. The extent to which an inventor may appropriate applications is fact-specific and often left to a jury; general rules cannot be universally laid down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive or unnecessary additions in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent 'contains more than is necessary to produce the described effect' and such addition appears to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public, that is a defence to an action on the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When it appears the patentee knowingly introduced something not useful, material, or necessary in preparing the specification, the patent may be vitiated under statute (Act of July 4, 1836, §15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of infringement (acts before issuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done before a patent is obtained are not infringements; the patent cannot be infringed by anything done when the patent did not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent is granted, the right relates back to the time of the invention so that a party who has practised the invention between discovery and issuing of the patent must cease to do so. Acts done after issuing of the patent will ground recovery, even if prior acts were done when it was uncertain a patent would issue. Relatedly, erection/use during a defective patent later surrendered and renewed: continuing use after renewal is infringement (no separate notice of renewal necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and manufacture under prior order — nominal damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Where patented articles were manufactured by defendants on an order from a third person and the order was partially executed before the defendants had notice of the patent, nominal damages only were proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, where merely the making of a patented machine is proved and no actual damages sustained, nominal damages should be given. Whoever erects or uses a patented machine does so at his peril, but lack of notice in some circumstances limits damages to nominal amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of 'actual damages' and statutory trebling
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual damages are such damages as the plaintiff can actually prove and has in fact sustained (as opposed to imaginary or vindictive damages); the court may render judgment for any sum above the amount found by verdict as actual damages, not exceeding three times the amount, according to the circumstances of the case (statutory treble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute allows the court to treble 'actual damages' (Act of July 4, 1836, §14). Actual damages should be proven; exemplary/vindictive damages are generally inappropriate except in special tort contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of actual damages for infringement by making and using
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of infringement by actual use (e.g., making and using a patented machine), actual damages are to give the value of such use during the time of the illegal user — i.e., the amount of profits actually received by the defendant — plus losses to which the plaintiff has been subjected by the piracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have differed on specific measures (e.g., price of machine), but the better course is to leave the matter to the jury to estimate actual damages according to the circumstances. Proper ingredients include the price of the machine, the nature, actual state and extent of the use, and particular losses 'valere quantum valcant.' If the plaintiff has been compelled to incur expenditures to establish his right, reasonable compensation for such expenditures (beyond taxable costs) may be allowed; counsel fees and witness expenses beyond taxable costs are now established to be allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal rule for damages; jury discretion and relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the difficulties in establishing a general rule, judges have sometimes left juries at large to estimate actual damages according to the circumstances of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factors include price of the machine, nature/extent of use, special losses suffered by the patentee, proofs in the cause; courts should avoid overly rigid universal measures that would be unjust in particular situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of verdicts on subsequent suits and equitable considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A verdict for the plaintiff does not necessarily transfer the patent right forever (the court cannot force defendant to purchase nor plaintiff to sell the patent right for the whole term merely by awarding price of machine); prior verdicts and acts done in reliance on them may be evidence in reduction of damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have been cautious about treating damages as a forced sale of the patent right; repeated suits and differing periods of infringement raise complex questions about legal bars and proper measure of damages; equitable considerations and the specific circumstances of consent or agreement at trial matter.
